At the edge of the harbor, where the water forgot its name, an old lighthouse blinked through the fog.

Each night, Mara climbed the spiral stairs and lit the lamp. Each morning, she found something new on the windowsill: a gull’s feather, a green bottle, once a tiny brass key warm as if someone had just held it.

She kept them all in a drawer.

Then, one winter night, the fog came in so thick that the lighthouse beam seemed to stop a few feet beyond the glass. Mara turned the lamp higher. Far out on the water, a light answered.

She hurried down to the shore. There, rocking gently in the dark, was a little boat with no sail and no oars. In it sat a child wearing a coat too large for him.

“Are you lost?” Mara called.

The child shook his head. “No,” he said. “I was looking for the light.”

Mara held out her hand. The child stepped onto the stones, and the boat drifted away by itself, carrying a small reflection of the moon.

Up in the lighthouse, the brass key fit a door Mara had never noticed, tucked behind the oldest shelf. It opened onto a narrow staircase that spiraled down, below the foundation, beneath the harbor floor.

At the bottom was a room full of windows. Through each one, Mara could see a different shore: a beach under red stars, a city built among clouds, a meadow where snow fell upward.

The child took her hand.

“You can come home now,” he said.

And for the first time in forty years, the lighthouse went dark—not because anyone had forgotten to light it, but because every shore had found its way.
